lifeCycle.label: High Growth
lifeCycle.question: Can growth keep scaling while margins rise toward where they'll settle?
lifeCycle.signature: Revenue still growing quickly, margins positive and improving, heavy reinvestment; free cash flow can still be thin or negative.
lifeCycle.pricing: Priced on revenue or forward earnings. The key question is whether the margin improvement the price assumes is actually showing up.

story: NVDA looks like a High Growth company, leaning toward Mature Growth (the app's rule of thumb, medium confidence).
Revenue grew +83.4% over the last twelve months at an operating margin of 65.2% (up +7.1 pp from a year earlier).
It turns 41.9% of revenue into free cash flow.
Each dollar invested in the business earned 320.2% after tax last year (ROIC).
That is +309.6 pp above what capital costs in its industry, so growth at these returns adds value.

foundations.title: Value vs price
foundations.question: If a stock's price doubles, did the company's value double?
foundations.what: Price is what the market pays today; value is what the business's future cash flows are worth, given their growth and risk.
foundations.why: Price is driven by mood, momentum and flows; value by fundamentals. They can drift apart for a long time — a trader profits from price, but knowing the fundamentals tells you what story the price is betting on.
caveats: Fundamentals rarely tell you when a price will move — they tell you what has to happen for the price to be justified.

lectures.title: Objective of the firm; value vs price

foundations.title: Corporate life cycle
foundations.question: Why would losing money be normal for one company and alarming for another?
foundations.what: Companies move through six stages — start-up, young growth, high growth, mature growth, mature stable, decline — and each stage has its own normal numbers.
foundations.why: The same reading means different things at different ages: negative free cash flow is the expected cost of growth for a young company and a red flag for a mature one. Placing the company first tells you which numbers matter most.
foundations.industry: Whole industries also age — but individual companies inside them can be at different stages.
caveats: The stage tag here is the app's rule of thumb from growth, margins and cash flow — Damodaran gives no numeric cut-offs.
Tech companies tend to age faster: they rise, peak and fade in fewer years.

lectures.title: Corporate Life Cycle class (20 short sessions)

foundations.title: Story and numbers
foundations.question: What would have to be true for today's price to make sense?
foundations.what: Every valuation is a story turned into four inputs: how fast revenue grows, what margins it reaches, how much it must reinvest to grow, and how risky it is.
foundations.why: If a piece of the story doesn't change one of those inputs, it isn't really part of the valuation. Checking what the price implies — growth, margins — is a quick way to see how much hope is priced in.
caveats: A bigger market only helps if the company can win a share of it profitably.

cards.title: Revenue growth
cards.question: Is fast revenue growth always good for shareholders?
cards.what: How much more the company sold than a year earlier. Trailing-twelve-month growth smooths seasons; the latest quarter shows the direction now; the 3-year figure shows the longer pattern.
cards.why: Growth only creates value when the money reinvested to get it earns more than it costs. Growth is the first lever in any valuation story, but it's never free.
cards.industry: Young industries (cloud software, new energy) grow fast as a whole; mature ones (food, utilities) grow near the economy's pace. Compare growth with peers, not with the market.
cards.stageNote: Still fast, usually 15–40%. The question is whether it's slowing gradually or falling off a cliff.
caveats: Acquisitions can make growth look organic when it was bought — check whether acquisitions show up in reinvestment.
One strong quarter after a weak one (easy comparison) can exaggerate the latest-quarter rate.

metrics.label: Revenue growth (TTM vs prior year)
metrics.formula: (Revenue TTM − Revenue of the 12 months before) ÷ Revenue of the 12 months before

metrics.label: Latest quarter revenue growth (vs same quarter last year)
metrics.formula: (This quarter's revenue − same quarter last year) ÷ same quarter last year

metrics.label: Revenue growth per year, last 3 fiscal years

bench.note: The industry figure is the 5-year growth rate; the company's is 3 years.

cards.title: Earnings growth
cards.question: Why can earnings grow much faster than revenue — and why doesn't that last?
cards.what: Growth in operating income (before interest and taxes) and in net income (what's left for shareholders).
cards.why: When margins expand, earnings outgrow revenue; that's what momentum traders often see in leaders. But margins can't expand forever, so long-run earnings growth comes back toward revenue growth.
cards.industry: Industries with high fixed costs (chips, airlines) see earnings swing much more than revenue — operating leverage works both ways.
cards.stageNote: Earnings growing faster than revenue is the signal that scale is paying off.
caveats: Growth from a near-zero or negative base produces huge, meaningless percentages.
Net income includes one-off items, interest and tax changes — operating income is the cleaner read of the business.

lectures.title: Cost of debt and capital; measuring earnings

metrics.label: Operating income growth (TTM)
metrics.formula: (Operating income TTM − prior 12 months) ÷ prior 12 months

metrics.label: Net income growth (TTM)
metrics.formula: (Net income TTM − prior 12 months) ÷ prior 12 months

cards.title: Gross margin
cards.question: What does gross margin tell you that operating margin doesn't?
cards.what: The share of each revenue dollar left after paying the direct cost of the product or service.
cards.why: It shows pricing power and the economics of the product itself, before the company spends on growth (R&D, marketing). A high gross margin with a negative operating margin means the product works but the company is spending heavily to grow.
cards.industry: Software and drug makers keep most of each dollar; retailers, distributors and manufacturers keep a small slice. A 30% gross margin is weak for software and strong for a grocer.
caveats: Companies decide what goes into cost of revenue differently, so compare within the industry only.

lectures.title: Cost of debt and capital; measuring earnings

metrics.label: Gross margin change vs a year ago
metrics.formula: Gross margin TTM − gross margin of the prior 12 months

cards.title: Operating margin
cards.question: If two companies grow equally fast, why might the one with lower margins be worth less?
cards.what: Operating income as a share of revenue — what the business earns from its operations before interest and taxes.
cards.why: It's the profitability input in a valuation story. The direction matters as much as the level: rising margins as the company grows is the payoff of scale; falling margins can signal competition or rising costs.
cards.industry: In Damodaran's January 2026 US data the pre-tax operating margin was about 33% for system & application software and about 2% for grocery retail — so 'good' depends entirely on the business.
cards.stageNote: Positive and rising toward the industry's typical level.
caveats: Damodaran treats R&D as an investment, not an expense — for R&D-heavy firms reported operating margins understate true profitability.
Under US accounting, operating lease costs sit inside operating income; his adjusted margins move them out. The industry comparison here uses his unadjusted column.

lectures.title: Cost of debt and capital; measuring earnings

metrics.label: Operating margin change vs a year ago
metrics.formula: Operating margin TTM − operating margin of the prior 12 months

cards.title: Net margin
cards.question: Why can two companies with the same operating margin have very different net margins?
cards.what: Net income as a share of revenue — what's left for shareholders after interest and taxes.
cards.why: It's what drives earnings per share, but it mixes the business (operating margin) with financing (interest) and one-off items, so it's a noisier read than operating margin.
cards.industry: Heavily indebted industries (utilities, telecom) lose more to interest, so their net margins sit further below operating margins.
caveats: One-off gains or write-downs can swing net income in a single year.
Compare with operating margin: a big gap means interest, tax or one-offs are doing the work.

lectures.title: Cost of debt and capital; measuring earnings

cards.title: R&D intensity
cards.question: Should research spending be treated like rent or like building a factory?
cards.what: Research and development spending as a share of revenue.
cards.why: Accounting subtracts R&D as an expense, but Damodaran argues it's an investment — spending today for products that earn for years. Treating it as capital usually raises margins and lowers return on capital for R&D-heavy firms.
cards.industry: Drug makers, chip designers and software firms spend heavily; retailers and utilities barely spend at all.
caveats: The app doesn't capitalize R&D yet — that adjustment (with an amortization life per industry) comes later.

lectures.title: Cost of debt and capital; measuring earnings

cards.title: Return on equity
cards.question: Can a company raise its ROE without becoming a better business?
cards.what: Net income as a share of the shareholders' equity on the balance sheet.
cards.why: It measures the return to shareholders on the money they have in the business. It's the main return measure for banks and insurers, where debt is part of the operation.
cards.industry: Asset-light businesses show high ROE; capital-heavy and regulated ones (banks, utilities) show lower ROE. Heavy buybacks shrink book equity and push ROE up mechanically.
caveats: More debt raises ROE without improving the business — compare with ROIC.
Negative book equity (common after large buybacks) makes ROE meaningless.

metrics.label: Return on equity (ROE)
metrics.formula: Net income TTM ÷ shareholders' equity a year earlier

cards.title: Return on invested capital
cards.question: Why can growth destroy value?
cards.what: After-tax operating income as a share of the capital invested in the business (debt + equity − cash), measured at the start of the year.
cards.why: This is the heart of Damodaran's corporate finance: a business creates value only when its return on capital beats its cost of capital. Growth at returns below that cost makes the company bigger and less valuable at the same time.
cards.industry: Asset-light businesses (software, brands) earn high returns on little capital; capital-heavy ones (utilities, steel, airlines) earn lower returns on a lot of capital. Compare with the industry and, ideally, with its cost of capital.
cards.stageNote: Rising return on capital is the sign that growth is becoming profitable.
caveats: Accounting choices (expensed R&D, leases, write-downs, buybacks) can push it far from the true economic return.
The next card compares it with what capital costs in the industry.

metrics.label: Return on invested capital (ROIC)
metrics.formula: Operating income × (1 − tax rate) ÷ (debt + equity − cash) a year earlier

cards.title: Returns vs the cost of capital
cards.question: Two companies both grow 20% a year. How can one be getting more valuable and the other less?
cards.what: The return the business earns on its capital minus the return its investors require for the risk (the cost of capital). For banks and insurers the same test is done on equity: return on equity minus the cost of equity.
cards.why: This spread is the hinge of corporate finance. Positive: every dollar reinvested is worth more than a dollar, so growth adds value. Zero: growth just makes the company bigger. Negative: growth destroys value, and the company would be worth more reinvesting less and returning cash.
cards.industry: Costs of capital differ by industry mainly through risk (beta) and debt: in Damodaran's January data, steady, debt-funded businesses such as utilities sit near the bottom and volatile, equity-funded ones such as semiconductors near the top. A 9% return clears the hurdle in one industry and misses it in another.
cards.stageNote: Turning positive is the moment growth starts creating value rather than just size.
caveats: The hurdle here is the industry's average cost of capital, not the company's own — a company with more debt or a riskier business has a different one.
One year of returns can be distorted by a write-down, a big acquisition or a cyclical peak.
Expensed R&D and leases make returns look different from their economic level, in either direction.

lectures.title: Cost of debt and capital; measuring earnings
Objective of the firm; value vs price

metrics.label: Return on capital minus cost of capital
metrics.formula: ROIC − the industry's cost of capital
metrics.note: Uses the industry's average cost of capital as the hurdle; a riskier or more indebted company has a different one.

cards.title: Free cash flow
cards.question: Why can a profitable company still run out of cash?
cards.what: Cash from operations minus spending on equipment and facilities (capex) — what's left after keeping and growing the asset base.
cards.why: Value comes from cash, not accounting earnings. A company with profits but negative free cash flow is reinvesting (or tying cash up in inventory and receivables); whether that's good depends on what the reinvestment earns.
cards.industry: Capital-heavy industries (chips manufacturing, energy, telecom) spend a lot on capex, so free cash flow trails earnings; software and services convert most earnings into cash.
cards.stageNote: Often still thin; turning positive is a milestone.
caveats: This is the simple version (operating cash flow − capex). Damodaran's FCFF starts from after-tax operating income and subtracts all reinvestment — shown on the Reinvestment card.
Operating cash flow adds back stock-based compensation; see the SBC card.

cards.title: Reinvestment
cards.question: Where does growth come from, and who pays for it?
cards.what: What the company puts back into the business: capex beyond depreciation, extra working capital, and acquisitions. The reinvestment rate is that amount as a share of after-tax operating income.
cards.why: Damodaran's link between growth and value: sustainable growth ≈ reinvestment rate × return on capital. A company that grows without reinvesting is either very efficient or living off past investment; one that reinvests heavily must earn good returns on it.
cards.industry: Asset-light industries reinvest little per dollar of growth; manufacturing, energy and telecom need a lot.
caveats: Acquisitions are lumpy — one deal can swing a single year.
FCFF here does not add back stock-based compensation, following Damodaran.

metrics.label: Reinvestment (TTM)
metrics.formula: (Capex − depreciation) + change in non-cash working capital + acquisitions

bench.note: His industry figure counts net capital spending (incl. acquisitions and R&D) but not working capital, so it's a close, not exact, match.

metrics.label: Free cash flow to the firm (Damodaran FCFF)

cards.title: Revenue to capital
cards.question: How much does it cost this company to add a dollar of revenue?
cards.what: Revenue per dollar of capital invested in the business.
cards.why: In Damodaran's story-to-numbers approach this ratio sets how much reinvestment a growth forecast needs: a high ratio means growth is cheap; a low one means every dollar of new revenue requires heavy investment.
cards.industry: Retailers and distributors turn capital over quickly (high ratio); utilities and telecom need lots of capital per dollar of revenue (low ratio).
cards.stageNote: The ratio decides how much cash growth will burn.
caveats: Damodaran publishes this ratio by industry without a written formula; revenue ÷ invested capital is the app's reading.
For forecasts he uses the marginal version — new revenue ÷ new capital — which can differ a lot from the average.

metrics.label: Revenue to invested capital
metrics.formula: Revenue TTM ÷ invested capital a year earlier (the app's reading of Damodaran's ratio)

cards.title: Stock-based compensation
cards.question: If a company pays employees in shares instead of cash, is that free?
cards.what: Pay given to employees in shares and options, as a share of revenue.
cards.why: Damodaran is firm that this is a real expense — paying in shares instead of cash still transfers value from existing shareholders. Adding it back to make 'adjusted' earnings or cash flow look better overstates what the business generates.
cards.industry: Heaviest in software and internet companies; small in industrial and consumer businesses.
caveats: Buybacks that only offset SBC dilution aren't really returning cash.

metrics.label: Free cash flow after stock compensation
metrics.formula: Free cash flow − stock-based compensation (SBC is a real cost paid in shares)

cards.title: Cash runway
cards.question: What happens when a cash-burning company's runway gets short?
cards.what: How many years the current cash pile lasts at the current rate of cash burn.
cards.why: For young companies the risk of failure is a real input in valuation. A short runway means new shares or debt soon — on whatever terms the market offers then.
caveats: Burn can change quickly as growth spending is cut or ramped up.

metrics.label: Cash runway at the current burn
metrics.formula: Cash and short-term investments ÷ yearly cash burn (negative free cash flow)

cards.title: Interest coverage
cards.question: How much could profits fall before interest payments become a problem?
cards.what: How many times operating income covers the year's interest expense.
cards.why: Damodaran uses coverage to estimate a 'synthetic' credit rating, and from it the company's cost of borrowing. Low coverage means a higher cost of debt and less room for bad years.
cards.industry: Stable businesses (utilities) can live with lower coverage than cyclical ones (chips, autos), whose profits can fall fast.
caveats: The rating table is Damodaran's January 2026 table for large non-financial firms; smaller, riskier firms use stricter bands.
Lease costs aren't counted as interest here.

lectures.title: Cost of debt and capital; measuring earnings

metrics.label: Implied credit rating (from coverage)
metrics.formula: Damodaran's coverage → rating table (January 2026, large non-financial firms)

cards.title: Debt load
cards.question: Is debt good or bad for a company?
cards.what: How much of the company is financed with debt (at market value), and how many years of operating cash profit (EBITDA) the debt equals.
cards.why: Debt brings a tax benefit and discipline, but adds the risk of distress. Damodaran's financing principle: choose the mix that minimizes the cost of capital — which depends on how stable the cash flows are.
cards.industry: Utilities, telecom and real estate carry lots of debt because their cash flows are steady; young tech firms carry little.
caveats: Damodaran counts operating leases as debt; the app shows them separately.
Net debt below zero means more cash than debt.

lectures.title: Debt vs equity; the financing trade-off
The cost of capital approach to debt

cards.title: Liquidity
cards.question: Can a company with plenty of assets still struggle to pay its bills?
cards.what: Current assets (cash, receivables, inventory) compared with bills due within a year.
cards.why: A short-term safety check: below 1 means near-term obligations exceed liquid assets.
cards.industry: Retailers and restaurants often run below 1 by design (customers pay before suppliers are paid); manufacturers usually run above it.
caveats: Inventory and receivables aren't cash — a high ratio built on slow-moving inventory is weaker than it looks.

lectures.title: Loose ends: cash, cross holdings, debt
Debt vs equity; the financing trade-off

metrics.label: Operating lease liabilities
metrics.formula: Lease liabilities on the balance sheet (Damodaran treats them as debt)

cards.title: Share count
cards.question: If profits grow 20% but the share count grows 10%, how much did each share's profit grow?
cards.what: How much the diluted number of shares changed in a year.
cards.why: New shares split the company into more pieces — each existing share owns less. Falling share counts (buybacks) do the opposite.
caveats: Convertible debt and options can add shares later.

lectures.title: Designing financing; first steps on dividends

metrics.label: Change in diluted share count (1 year)
metrics.formula: Diluted shares now ÷ diluted shares a year ago − 1

cards.title: Cash returned
cards.question: When should a company pay out cash instead of reinvesting it?
cards.what: Buybacks plus dividends over the last year, and that amount compared with free cash flow.
cards.why: Damodaran's dividend principle: return cash when there aren't enough investments that earn more than the cost of capital. Paying out more than the company generates is borrowing to return cash; paying out nothing while sitting on cash raises the question of what management will do with it.
cards.industry: Mature consumer, energy and financial companies return the most; growing tech firms return little.
caveats: Buybacks that just offset stock-based compensation aren't a true return.
Over 100% of free cash flow is financed by debt or cash on hand.

lectures.title: Designing financing; first steps on dividends
Dividend policy: facts and schools of thought

metrics.label: Cash returned as % of free cash flow

cards.title: What the market pays
cards.question: Is a company with a P/E of 60 always expensive?
cards.what: How many dollars the market pays for a dollar of revenue, of earnings, and of operating income (counting debt and cash).
cards.why: Multiples are pricing, not valuation — they show what the market is betting on. A high multiple needs high growth, high returns on capital and low risk to be justified; Damodaran's test is to check those fundamentals before calling a multiple high or low.
cards.industry: Multiples are only comparable within an industry and after controlling for growth and risk.
caveats: The app's peer comparison uses the data provider's multiples for consistency.

lectures.title: Objective of the firm; value vs price

bench.note: Industry figure: total market cap ÷ total net income of the profitable firms.

metrics.label: EV to operating income
metrics.formula: (Market cap + debt − cash) ÷ operating income TTM
